summary: Redwood demo focused on evaluation and quality monitoring: how to build prompt sets, set regression alerts, and run A/B comparisons in Console + Optimize. Customer is evaluating for a pilot; key concerns: regression false positives, data residency, and how to operationalize periodic benchmarks. Agreed next steps: share runbook and sample prompt set, customer to provide queries, plan benchmark run.
topics: Metric selection (semantic similarity, accuracy, hallucination rate)
transcript:
[00:00] Liam Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Uh, quick roll call — I have Priya and Zoe here from Redwood.
[00:07] Marta Ruiz: Morning — thanks, Liam. Marta here, and I have Derek and Angela on as well.
[00:13] Liam Chen: Great. Goal for today is a focused walkthrough of our evaluation tooling — prompt sets, regression alerts, and the A/B compare flow in the Console and Optimize. We'll also cover how you'd run a pilot and what artifacts you need. Does that sound right?
[00:26] Angela Kim: Yes, that's exactly what we need. We're trying to codify quality checks for our clinical triage assistant before we expand.
[00:33] Priya Narayan: Awesome, we'll jump into the Console demo in a sec. Quick context question — Marta, do you already have a canonical prompt template or a set of golden outputs?
[00:41] Marta Ruiz: We have a mix. There are a few canonical prompts product uses in prod. But, um, we don't have labeled gold outputs for everything, which is one of the gaps.
[00:50] Derek Shaw: Also important — we need to keep the data in our EU region. Any caching or export has to comply with our residency rules.
[00:58] Priya Narayan: Noted — Redwood supports region-bound evaluation runs and you can keep eval artifacts in your private storage via our Private offering. We'll show how the Console marks dataset residency.
[01:08] Liam Chen: Ok, quick agenda: 1) how to construct a prompt set and tagging; 2) running baseline evaluations; 3) setting regression alerts and tuning thresholds; 4) A/B compare and exportable diffs. Priya, you want to share your screen?
[01:21] Priya Narayan: Yep. (screen share starts) All right, Console landing page — you can see the 'Evals' tab.
[01:27] Priya Narayan: First step is a prompt-set. This is a curated CSV where each row is: prompt_id, prompt_text, metadata (intent, sensitivity), expected_output (optional), and tags. We recommend including at least one "gold" expected_output for each high-sensitivity path.
[01:44] Angela Kim: How do you handle variable slots? We have prompts that take patient symptoms as slot values.
[01:50] Priya Narayan: Great question. You can parameterize prompts: include a template and then a set of example slot values. The eval runner will expand them and treat each expansion as a single test case. That way you get coverage across permutations.
[02:03] Marta Ruiz: And for scoring — if we don't have a gold, can we do similarity-based scoring?
[02:07] Priya Narayan: Yes. We support multiple scorers: exact-match, token-based (ROUGE-L style), and embedding-similarity (cosine) for semantic checks. You can combine scorers and assign weights — e.g., 0.7 semantic, 0.3 token overlap.
[02:19] Derek Shaw: What about hallucination detection? Any out-of-the-box heuristics?
[02:23] Priya Narayan: We provide a hallucination detector plugin that's based on fact-checking against a provided knowledge source or knowledge cutoff. For clinical content you can plug your internal KB and we run evidence overlap checks; we also provide a model-agnostic hallucination score you can tune.
[02:36] Liam Chen: Ok moving into regression alerts. In Console you choose a baseline run (say, model v1.3) and then create a monitor that will compare subsequent deployments against it.
[02:47] Priya Narayan: Here's the monitor create flow — you set evaluation frequency (daily, weekly), choose the metric(s), and then configure alert thresholds either as absolute values or relative tolerances. For example: semantic_similarity_mean drop > 4% or hallucination_rate increase > 1.5% triggers an alert.
[03:03] Angela Kim: We get a lot of small fluctuations; how do we avoid noisy alerts?
[03:07] Priya Narayan: Two levers: (1) aggregation window — you can require a sustained degradation over N runs; (2) p-value-based statistical test — Console can apply a Welch's t-test or bootstrap to reduce false positives. Most customers prefer a rolling 7-day window plus a minimum sample size.
[03:23] Marta Ruiz: Do you support custom metrics, like a weighted business metric we compute in-house?
[03:28] Priya Narayan: Absolutely — bring your metric via a webhook or upload a CSV of scores. Console can ingest and incorporate it into alerts.
[03:35] Liam Chen: Now A/B compare: you can spin up two model variants or two prompt configurations. Optimize will run them against the same prompt-set and produce a paired-diff report.
[03:45] Priya Narayan: (shows example) We run A and B simultaneously; outputs are aligned by prompt_id. The report highlights top regressions, delta in semantic similarity, and example pairs with side-by-side outputs. You can export a delta CSV or a human-friendly review queue to triage.
[03:59] Derek Shaw: If we run this in our VPC, does the data leave our network?
[04:03] Priya Narayan: For Private deployments all evaluation traffic can be kept inside your VPC — logs and artifacts can be written to your S3 bucket in-region; Redwood's control plane just records metadata if you opt in.
[04:12] Angela Kim: Can we automate rollbacks? Like if a new model fails the monitor, automatically revert to previous staged model?
[04:18] Priya Narayan: Yes — Console exposes a rollout policy where you can specify automatic fallback if a monitor trips. You can also configure canary sizes and automatic throttling.
[04:27] Marta Ruiz: Show us an example alert email or Slack notification.
[04:30] Priya Narayan: (switches view) Here's the alert page — you can route to Slack, PagerDuty, or webhook. Email includes a summary, top-k regression examples, and a link to the triage queue. The Slack message has quick actions: view diff, mute, create ticket.
[04:45] Zoe Park: (interject) We also attach a permalink to the exact eval run, with diffs and the raw token-level breakdown, so your docs/engineering team can reproduce.
[04:53] Marta Ruiz: That permalink — is it accessible to external reviewers? We sometimes share with clients.
[04:57] Priya Narayan: Permalinks are access-controlled via SSO and RBAC. For sharing you can generate an expiring public link with or without redaction.
[05:07] Angela Kim: How do you handle prompt drift over time?
[05:10] Priya Narayan: We recommend scheduling periodic re-evals and also running an unsupervised drift detector on prompt distributions. Console flags prompt templates whose outputs diverge in embedding space beyond a threshold; then you can add them to a manual review queue.
[05:23] Marta Ruiz: Sounds useful; do you have a recommended run cadence for our use-case — clinical triage?
[05:28] Liam Chen: For high-sensitivity workflows we usually recommend nightly smoke runs on a reduced prompt-set and a full weekly run on the complete set, plus immediate post-deploy checks for canaries.
[05:37] Derek Shaw: On the pilot — we're leaning to test hosted first to get metrics, then move to dedicated or private if we like the perf. Any gotchas?
[05:45] Liam Chen: Hosted is fastest for iteration, but you trade strict residency and certain compliance controls. Dedicated gives predictable throughput; Private gives residency and network controls. For your timeline, a hosted pilot followed by a Dedicated reservation is common.
[05:58] Marta Ruiz: Can you run the A/B now with a tiny sample? We brought a small prompt-set (20 rows) to see the flow.
[06:05] Priya Narayan: Sure let's do a quick smoke. Uploading the CSV now... (typing) All right, selecting model A (redwood/gpt-lite-4q), model B (redwood/gpt-lite-4q-quant) — launching paired run.
[06:20] Angela Kim: How long for 20?
[06:22] Priya Narayan: Should be under a minute. It runs in parallel and we stream results.
[06:30] (brief pause, typing)
[06:36] Priya Narayan: Results streaming — semantic similarity: A mean 0.87, B mean 0.84. Top regression: prompt_id 12, B dropped 0.22. Here's the side-by-side output for that prompt — you can see the quantized variant truncates a clarifying clause.
[06:52] Marta Ruiz: That's exactly the kind of thing we'd catch. Can we annotate that example as a 'must-fix'?
[06:58] Priya Narayan: Yep, you can flag and send to your engineering queue or create a bug directly in Jira via our integration.
[07:05] Derek Shaw: About costs — do you show per-token cost for these runs?
[07:08] Priya Narayan: We do — the run summary includes token count, runtime, and estimated cost broken down by model and by token type (prompt vs completion).
[07:17] Angela Kim: One of our concerns is false positives from small sample sizes. How do we set the sample threshold?
[07:22] Priya Narayan: On the monitor you can set minimum sample size. For example, require at least 200 examples per day before alerts fire. We also recommend using a lower-sensitivity mode for early phases.
[07:33] Liam Chen: Quick commercial note — pilot pricing is consumption-based with an option to reserve Dedicated capacity if you need consistent latency. I'll send a worksheet.
[07:41] Marta Ruiz: Regarding security docs — is SOC 2 and ISO listed somewhere?
[07:45] Zoe Park: Yes, we'll attach the security pack in the follow-up pack; we also have a Private deployment checklist for KMS/HSM and SSO.
[07:54] Angela Kim: If we opt for Private, what is the typical lead time?
[07:57] Priya Narayan: Private deployments are usually 4–8 weeks depending on network approvals and on-prem requirements. Dedicated is faster — often a week for capacity reservation.
[08:06] Marta Ruiz: Ok, back to the runbook — can you explain the recommended metric set for clinical triage?
[08:12] Priya Narayan: We recommend a combo: semantic_similarity_mean, hallucination_rate, response_length_range, and a business-weighted accuracy where you tag critical-responses and require stricter thresholds. For safety, add an abstain-rate target when model returns uncertain answers.
[08:26] Derek Shaw: On abstain — can you force a fallback to a safe response or escalate to human?
[08:30] Priya Narayan: Yes — you can configure a rule: if semantic_similarity < 0.6 or hallucination_score > 0.4 then route to human review or return a templated safe response.
[08:40] Angela Kim: Can we backfill historical logs into Console for trend analysis?
[08:44] Priya Narayan: You can upload historical runs (CSV/NDJSON) and the system will compute trend lines and integrate with the monitors. Private runs can be ingested from your S3 as well.
[08:54] Liam Chen: Let's do a quick walkthrough of the triage queue — after a run you get a list sorted by severity. You can mark 'accepted', 'rejected', or 'needs-investigation'.
[09:04] Priya Narayan: (shows triage) For each flagged example you can open the token-level analyzer, see attention spans (approx), KV cache notes, and reproduction steps. Helps SEs debug prompt/temperature/kv cache interactions.
[09:20] Marta Ruiz: A question on A/B: do you randomize by user or by prompt? We have stateful sessions; randomizing per prompt might not be valid.
[09:29] Priya Narayan: Good call — Optimize supports per-session bucketing for stateful flows. You can also seed the session so both variants get equivalent histories for fair comparison.
[09:39] Derek Shaw: For the pilot we'll probably want to do a session-level A/B with a 10% traffic canary.
[09:44] Liam Chen: Sounds reasonable. We'll include a recommended rollout plan in the follow-up materials.
[09:50] Angela Kim: Any gotchas on embedding-based metrics? We use two different embedding models internally.
[09:55] Priya Narayan: Use the same embedder for both baseline and new runs to keep the metric consistent. Console supports specifying the embedding model; we also provide model mapping guidance.
[10:05] Marta Ruiz: Let's talk about false positives again — can you show an example where the system suppresses noise with the statistical test?
[10:11] Priya Narayan: (runs a demo) Here I have two runs with small deltas. With the default threshold you'd get an alert; if we apply the bootstrap with 1000 resamples and require p < 0.05, the alert is suppressed. It's surfaced as low-confidence drift instead.
[10:27] Angela Kim: Nice. What does the audit log look like? We need traceability for compliance.
[10:31] Zoe Park: Audit logs capture run metadata, who created monitors, thresholds changes, and who acknowledged alerts. They can be forwarded to your SIEM or long-term storage for 7+ years depending on retention plan.
[10:41] Derek Shaw: How are PII and redaction handled in the eval artifacts?
[10:45] Priya Narayan: We provide automatic redaction options for PHI/PII fields at ingestion, plus configurable redaction rules. For Private, you can choose to never persist raw inputs — only store hashed IDs and metrics.
[10:55] Marta Ruiz: This is all good. Two final questions: (1) can we schedule the live benchmark with you? (2) do you have an example contract addendum for pilot data handling?
[11:04] Liam Chen: Yes to both. Priya will own the benchmark run scheduling; Zoe will attach the pilot addendum and security pack.
[11:12] Priya Narayan: I'll follow up with calendar options. Also attaching the Eval Runbook link: https://redwood-inference.com/docs/evals/runbook (sample prompt-set template included).
[11:23] Angela Kim: Perfect.
[11:25] Marta Ruiz: Thanks everyone — this was helpful.
[11:28] Liam Chen: Quick recap: we'll share runbook + prompt-set template; NovaCare provides 200 anonymized queries and 3 prompt templates; we'll schedule a paired A/B benchmark for the week of 2026-10-19. Anyone object?
[11:41] Derek Shaw: No objections.
[11:43] Angela Kim: Looks good.
[11:45] Zoe Park: I'll attach SOC 2 and Private checklist in the email.
[11:48] Liam Chen: Great — thanks all, we'll follow up via email and update the CRM.
[11:52] (meeting ends)
